extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, students learning English grammar and usage
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and descriptive rules for English sentence structure, word usage, punctuation, and style aimed at improving clarity, correctness, and euphony in written English. Covers sentence openings, conjunctions, interjections, clause types, negation, expletives, parallelism, clefts, article use, and other usage points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning a sentence with 'but'
rubrics_metrics.description: But is a perfectly proper way to open a sentence, but only if the idea it introduces truly contrasts with what precedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use but to open a sentence or a paragraph when the idea introduced is explicitly contrastive; avoid using it where there is no real contrast. Example: effective paragraph opening that develops an idea contrary to the one preceding it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning a sentence with 'however'
rubrics_metrics.description: However has been used as a conjunctive adverb since the fourteenth century and, like other adverbs, can be used at the beginning of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the simple but for stronger impact; however is more ponderous and often more effective within a sentence to emphasize what precedes it (e.g., 'Soon, however, it turned out...'). For euphony many writers shun sentence-starting however, though it is fine in the sense 'in whatever way' when not followed by a comma (e.g., 'however that may be').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunctions and verb number
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinating and disjunctive conjunctions affect whether a verb should be plural or singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'And' and 'through' typically impart plurality so use a plural verb (e.g., 'the first through seventh innings were scoreless'). 'Or' and 'either-or' distinguish elements and do not impart plurality—use singular if elements are singular. Some conjunctions (e.g., and used copulatively) may not affect number; check context. See also cross-reference to related rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interjections defined
rubrics_metrics.description: An interjection or exclamation is a word, phrase, or clause that denotes strong feeling and has little or no grammatical function in a sentence; it is used absolutely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interjections may stand alone as sentences (e.g., 'Oh! I've lost my wallet!') and are distinguished by punctuation. Compare meanings depending on punctuation and placement (e.g., 'Well, I didn't know him' vs 'I didn't know him well'). See related rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interjections
rubrics_metrics.description: Interjections are natural in speech and frequently used in dialogue; as a midsentence interrupter, an interjection may direct attention to phrasing or reflect attitude, especially in informal/colloquial tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interjections to convey tone or interruption (e.g., 'our business proposal was, ahem, poorly presented'). They are particularly appropriate for commands, exclamations, or dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interjections and functional variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because interjections are usually grammatically independent, all other parts of speech may be used as interjections (exclamatory noun, adjective, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that words categorized as other parts of speech can function as interjections (examples: 'good!','idiot!','help!','indeed!','me!','and!','quickly!'). Adjust punctuation and tone accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words that are exclusively interjections
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words are used only as interjections—for example, ouch, whew, ugh, psst, and oops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as standalone exclamatory elements; punctuation and spacing guide their integration into prose or dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntax denotes the rules governing how words are arranged into sentences; in analytic English, word order is particularly important in expressing meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand English's reliance on word order (SVO) to convey relations; departures typically signal emphasis or questions. Use syntactic rules to avoid ambiguity and to craft intended emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements (declarative sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sentences are statements with a declarative structure in which the clause contains a subject and the subject precedes the verb; sometimes the subject is implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize implied-subject constructions in informal speech ('[he] missed the ball') and note exceptional negative idioms where the subject may follow part of the verb ('scarcely had we arrived...'). Ensure clarity when eliding subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Three main types of questions: (1) yes-no questions, (2) wh- questions (who, what, when, where, why, which, how), and (3) alternative questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form each type according to interrogative structure (e.g., question words for wh- questions). Use examples for expected form and response patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional types of questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Four interrogative utterances not classifiable under the three categories: rising-pitch declarative questions, tag questions, exclamatory questions, and rhetorical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rising pitch to indicate a question with declarative structure; tag questions append an interrogative tag ('hasn't he?'); exclamatory questions may use falling intonation and exclamation points; rhetorical questions make emphatic statements without expectation of an answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directives (imperatives) and their types
rubrics_metrics.description: A directive or imperative instructs somebody to do or not to do something; there are eight main types: command, prohibition, invitation, warning, plea, request, well-wishing, and advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate imperative form to match force and nuance (e.g., 'come here now!' vs 'join us for dinner!'). Different punctuation and tone signal different directive types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional directives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some directives depart from common patterns, for example when the subject is expressed, when they begin with let ('let's have a picnic'), or when they begin with do ('do help yourself').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and correctly punctuate or structure these variants; consider register and intended politeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclamation expresses how moved or impressed a speaker is; it can be a simple interjection or follow sentence structures (what/how + subject + verb) and sometimes uses inverted word order for formal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exclamations for emphasis or stylistic effect ('What an extraordinary novel this is!'); in formal literary English, inverted order ('Little did I expect...') is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple sentence consists of a single independent clause with no dependent clause, and can still contain internal compound constructions serving as subjects, verbs, or objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that a simple sentence maintains a single independent clause (e.g., 'no man is an island'). Avoid misidentifying compound predicates as compound sentences unless a subject is elided and intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound sentence contains two independent (coordinate) clauses with no dependent clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of debate over whether sentences like 'She arrived early and stayed late' are simple with a compound predicate or compound with elided subject; be consistent in analysis and punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex sentence contains a single independent clause with one or more dependent clauses (adjective, noun, or adverbial clauses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify dependent clauses and their functions (e.g., adjective clause 'that were nominated', noun clause 'that most behavioral differences...'). Use subordination to combine related ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound-complex sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound-complex sentence contains multiple independent clauses and at least one dependent clause; it differs from a complex sentence by having more than one independent clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coordination and subordination appropriately; ensure clarity when multiple clauses are combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of word order (SVO)
rubrics_metrics.description: English is analytic and depends largely on word order—basic subject-verb-object (SVO) governs meaning; departures typically signal emphasis or a question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain SVO order for clarity; when deviating, do so intentionally to create emphasis or interrogative force. Examples illustrate how meaning changes when order changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: All seven syntactic patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Clause patterns are limited to specific types that include combinations of subject (S), verb (V), object (O), indirect object (IO), complement (C), adverbial (A); all seven basic patterns are listed (S+V, S+V+O, S+V+C, S+V+A, S+V+IO+O, S+V+OO+C, S+V+OO+A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these patterns to diagnose clause function and to construct grammatically balanced sentences; label sentence elements when analyzing structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations on syntactic order (inversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: When clause elements appear in a different order, inversion may indicate a question (V-S-C) or special emphasis (e.g., 'Yoda my name is!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inversion sparingly for emphasis because it departs from normal sequence; expect reader attention when inversion is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clauses (definition and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause contains a subject, a finite verb, and any complements required by the verb; independent clauses can stand alone, dependent clauses cannot and are introduced by relative pronouns or subordinating conjunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize clause types and their roles (direct object, adjectival, adverbial) when constructing sentences to ensure grammatical correctness and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative clauses and contact (whiz-deletion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relative clause is introduced by a relative pronoun and modifies a noun element; contact clauses omit the relative pronoun (a type of elliptical clause often involving whiz-deletion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relative clauses to modify nouns; be mindful of contact clauses and possible ambiguity when the relative pronoun is omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appositive clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: An appositive clause is used in apposition to a noun element and, unlike a relative clause, is self-contained and could stand on its own if the introductory relative pronoun were removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish appositive clauses from restrictive relative clauses; punctuation and clause independence affect meaning and flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional clauses (protasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conditional clause (protasis) is an adverbial clause typically introduced by if or unless and establishes the condition on which the main clause depends; conditions may be open (real) or hypothetical (unreal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft conditional sentences to convey intended modality: open (factual/possible) vs hypothetical (contrary-to-fact). Use appropriate tense and subordinators (if, unless, should, although, etc.). Examples show direct, indirect, alternative, and open-range conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis (grammatical omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis occurs when part of a clause is left understood and the reader/listener supplies missing words; recovery is possible due to context and the principle of recoverability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ellipsis to avoid repetition and shorten messages, especially suitable for commands/exclamations and in answers that would otherwise repeat a question. Distinguish grammatical ellipsis from omitted text in quotations (ellipsis dots). Examples illustrate how omitted material is recovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation (general types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation reverses expression in a sentence; four common types are: (1) using the negative particle not/no, (2) negating pronouns/adverbs (nobody, never), (3) coordinating conjunctions neither/nor, (4) words negative in meaning or with negative affixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate negation strategy to express scope and avoid ambiguity; be aware of affixal negatives (un-, dis-, non-, -less) and negative-meaning words (few, little, rarely). Examples of each type provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and placement of 'not'
rubrics_metrics.description: Not typically negates a verb, object, phrase, or clause and usually precedes the element being negated; with ordinary verbs in present/past indicative, replace verb with do/did + not + bare infinitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With multiple verbs in a negative, not usually follows the first auxiliary. With participial phrases, not precedes the participle. Note contraction forms (-n't) and exceptions (am — no contraction with negative; cannot vs can't; will not vs won't; shan't rare in American English). Examples show scope changes depending on placement ('He definitely did not accept' vs 'He did not definitely accept').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'no'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No' negates only adjectives and nouns and can produce ambiguity when combined with adjective phrases (e.g., 'no fresh eggs for sale').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'no' carefully when modifying adjectives to avoid ambiguity about whether something is entirely absent or absent in a particular quality/state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using pronouns and adverbs for negation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns (nobody, none, no one, nothing) and adverbs (nowhere, never) negate without using not and can reduce wordiness and improve flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer these forms when they yield clearer or more concise sentences (e.g., 'We saw no one' vs 'We did not see anyone').

rubrics_metrics.name: Using 'neither' and 'nor'
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither and nor negate alternatives simultaneously; traditionally used for pairs, but writers sometimes extend them (neither-nor-nor) with three or more elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For three or more elements, sequence neither-nor-nor is preferable to avoid ambiguity. Examples show conventional and extended usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative interrogative and imperative statements
rubrics_metrics.description: In negative interrogatives, the first auxiliary may be contracted with not (Aren't you...?) or left uncontracted ('Are you not...'); in an imperative, the negative particle follows the imperative verb or is contracted with it ('don't talk back!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select contraction and placement to match register and intended force; punctuation signals tone (question mark or exclamation point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: In Standard English two negatives usually cancel to a mild positive; in some dialects multiple negatives intensify negation—multiple negatives often lead to ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid multiple negatives in Standard English unless dialectal voice is intended; be mindful of potential ambiguity about the expected outcome (e.g., 'I wouldn't be surprised if Dan doesn't find the hammer').

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Any' vs 'some' in negative statements
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Any' words must be used with the negating particle not; 'some' words aren't used with not in standard negative constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'any' in negative contexts ('I don't want to see anybody'), not 'some' ('I don't want to see somebody' is incorrect unless a specific unnamed person is meant). Examples contrast wrong/right usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expletives (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: In grammar, an expletive is a word that has no lexical meaning but serves a merely structural role in a sentence (commonly 'it' and 'there').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expletive it or there to shift emphasis to the predicate; distinguish expletive there from adverbial there of place. Examples illustrate anticipatory uses ('It is not known what happened'; 'There are many viewpoints...'). Avoid clashing repeated its in a passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expletive 'it'
rubrics_metrics.description: Expletive it adds no meaning and takes the subject's or object's place when the real subject shifts to the predicate (e.g., 'It is foolish to ignore facts' = 'Ignoring facts is foolish').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers usually distinguish pronoun it from expletive it by context; avoid multiple nearby its that cause stumbling. Other names: ambient it, anticipatory it, dummy it, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expletive 'there'
rubrics_metrics.description: There is used as an expletive with be or intransitive/linking verbs followed by the subject ('There are many different viewpoints...'); it should not be confused with there as an adverb of place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expletive there to introduce existence or presence; ensure reader can distinguish from locative there by context and word order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel structure (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel constructions are series of like sentence elements; every element of a parallel series must be a functional match (word, phrase, clause, sentence) and serve the same grammatical function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain functional matching to avoid syntactic breakdown. Examples of poor vs better constructions illustrate mismatches and corrections. Check lists, series, and correlative structures for parallelism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositions and parallel structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In a parallel series of prepositional phrases, repeat the preposition with every element unless they all use the same preposition; failure to do so can be jarring or ungrammatical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat prepositions when appropriate ('in the sock drawer, in the laundry hamper, in the bathroom, and under the bed') or use a single preposition only when it naturally applies to all objects in the series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paired joining terms and parallel structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlative conjunctions (either-or, neither-nor, both-and, not only-but also) and some adverb pairs must join grammatically parallel sentence elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure both parts of the correlative are parallel in form; correct mismatches by rephrasing (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary verbs and parallel structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If an auxiliary verb appears before a series of verb phrases, it must apply to all of them; otherwise the series may be ungrammatical or nonsensical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either restructure the series so the auxiliary applies to all items or break out items into separate sentences. Examples show how to fix mismatched auxiliaries and tense shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleft sentences defined
rubrics_metrics.description: A cleft sentence opens with a subject clause (it-clause, what-clause, etc.) to change focus by adding words (it, was, who; there, are, that; or what and was).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cleft sentences to emphasize new information (actor, object, time/place). Examples show shifting focus (e.g., 'It was Manuel who met Adam...'). Clefts can be reduced when the information is understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of cleft sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A cleft sentence may be declarative, interrogative, positive, or negative; the relative pronoun is often elided in a whiz-deletion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose cleft type according to communicative goal; use elision when context makes the pronoun redundant. Examples show positive and negative clefts and their reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cleft sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleft sentences are sometimes used for dramatic effect to signal a shift or beginning and may imply contrast or mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ clefts for emphasis or to create interesting leads; be cautious of unintended implications (e.g., 'It's not Joan who wants to be a social activist' implies distinction or mistake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar versus usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Many issues writers/editors face concern usage—the collective habits of native speakers—rather than grammar; dictionaries describe usage but do not always indicate fitness for Standard Written English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult style or usage guides (Fowler's, Garner's) in the publishing world to decide appropriateness for print. Use judgment when dictionaries record nonstandard or questionable forms (examples: infer vs imply; irregardless recorded but not recommended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article use: 'a' vs 'an'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the indefinite article 'a' before any word beginning with a consonant sound and 'an' before any word beginning with a vowel sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose based on pronunciation (sound), not spelling. Special cases: words like 'historical' depend on whether the /h/ is pronounced; initialisms (letters sounded out) take 'an' or 'a' accordingly, while acronyms (pronounced as words) follow vowel/consonant sound rule (example: 'an HTML website' vs 'a HUD program').
